lines: You're not family. There isn't any. You'll do.
Mr Coram died on Friday. Somebody has to tell his bees, or they'll go. You knock on each hive and tell them. Plainly, mind.
Knock on the roof of each and say it plain. Three hives. They don't like being kept waiting.
Cut? Nobody's been near those hives. I'd have heard. I don't sleep.
Here. His honey, from last year. He'd want it eaten, not looked at.
Somebody's cutting his comb. Cleanly, you said. The way he did it.
Wait by the hives after the bell and see who it is. I'll not. I don't go out after the bell. Nobody sensible does.
After the bell, by the hives. Stand still and they'll leave you be.
A man in a veil. At his hives. At night.
Then they've not been told properly, and nor has he. It's crepe you want, black, round each hive. That tells them for certain.
Or you leave him to it. I'd not blame you either way.
Then I'll leave him be.
He always left me a jar on the step, when there was honey. I dare say he'll go on.
Round each of the three. Knot it at the back, where the wind won't have it.
Then that's done. They know, and so does he.
Nobody'll cut the comb now. They can keep it this year.
The crepe's holding. They're quieter, if anything.
I've taken his veil in, stake and all. It was only getting wet.
He leaves a jar on the step. I let it stand a day before I take it. It seems only fair.

tale_coram.speaker: A Man in a Bee Veil

lines: He is cutting comb by feel, without a light, and does not look up.
Evening. Mind the slot, they're still coming in.
It wants doing before the frost, and nobody else will. They know me.
That's the name on the board.
Go on home. It's no night to be out in, and I'm nearly done.
Evening. There'll be a jar on the step for her by morning.
Don't tell her it's from me. She knows.
A white hive on legs. Bees come and go at the slot along the bottom.
You knock twice on the roof of the hive and tell them that Mr Coram died on Friday.
The hum does not change.
They have been told. The hum is low and even.
You tie a length of black crepe round the hive and knot it at the back, where the wind will not have it.
Black crepe round the hive, knotted at the back. The bees come and go under it.

Lifting the roof to knock, you see comb cut from the frames inside. The cut edges are fresh.
The hum does not change.
They have been told. Somebody has cut comb from this one, cleanly, with a warm knife.

Black crepe round the hive, knotted at the back. The bees come and go under it.
A bee veil on a stake by the door: a wide hat, and a net darned in two places.
The net is damp, as if it had been out in the dew.
A stake with a nail in the top. There is nothing on the nail.
You knock. Nobody answers. The door is locked, and the key is not under the mat. There is no mat.
A jar of honey on the step, full to the shoulder, with a clean lid. HANNEY is written on the lid in pencil.
Mrs Pollard. You'll excuse the curlers. I've not been to bed properly since Easter.
My husband walks in his sleep. After the bell, most nights. I tie a bell on his ankle so I hear him go.
Would you follow him tonight? See where he gets to. I can't keep up, and I don't like the dark.
After the bell he comes out of the front door and stands a while, and then he goes. You'll hear the bell.
A stone. A dinner, under a cloth.
He's not asleep, is he. He never was.
Our Tom's been up at the School since the winter. He never would eat what they gave him.

options.label: Shall I bring the plate back?

lines: Yes. Bring it back. No plate, no going.
Don't tell him I sent you. Not that it matters. He'll know.
Then I'll do two plates. One from each of us.
He can carry both. He's steady enough, when he's going there.
The stone's north of the house, not far. The plate's my good one, with the blue rim.
That's my good plate.
He'll sit in tonight, then. He'll sit in the chair by the door and listen for the bell, and I'll sit with him.
He sits in the chair by the door now, nights, and listens for the bell. I sit with him. We don't say much.
Two plates on the stone, and both of them clean by morning.
Don't ask me who. I don't.
Evening. Don't mind me.
I'll not be long. I never am.
He stands by the stone, his coat buttoned over his pyjamas. The bell on his ankle is still.
"It's for our Tom. He's up at the School. He comes down for it when I've gone. He always does."
"Go on home. It's cold, and you've no bell on."
Evening. She's in with the kettle.
I'm listening. You can hear the School from here at nine, if the wind's right. I like to know it's rung.
A flat stone set on two others, waist high. Cut into the edge: THE DOLE STONE. ANYBODY IN NEED, TAKE AND GIVE THANKS.
A dinner plate on the stone, under a cloth. Under the cloth: mutton, potatoes, gravy gone to a skin, and a knife and fork laid straight.
A plate with a blue rim on the stone, under a cloth. Under the cloth it is wiped clean, the knife and fork laid across it.
Mrs Pollard's good plate, with the blue rim, wiped clean.
The Dole Stone, bare. There are crumbs on it, and a clean ring where a plate stood.
A second plate beside the first, on a stone of its own, under its own cloth. Bread and dripping, cut into soldiers.
The door is on the latch. Inside, a clock is ticking, and there is a smell of gravy.
A kitchen chair outside the door, a blanket folded on the seat. The ground under it is worn to bare earth.
The slippers are not by the step.
A man's carpet slippers by the step, worn through at the toes. There is grass seed in them.
He's gone again. Horace. My tortoise. He was my father's, and his father's before that, near enough.
Follow the dandelions. He takes a bite out of each as he goes, and he doesn't go fast. He's ninety.
Bitten dandelions. He always goes the same way. North, up past the house.
Horace. You old fool.
North again. Every autumn, the same. He's never got far. One year he will.
He gets out by the front of his box. Pushes past it, slow as you like.
There's a flat stone beside it. Push it up against the front for me, and I'll fetch him out of the kitchen after. My back won't push anything these days.
The flat stone, up against the front of the box. Push, don't lift. I've got him in the kitchen till it's done.
That'll hold him.
In you go, Horace. There. Nose to the stone. That's your winter.
That'll hold him.
In you go, Horace. There. Nose to the stone. That's your winter.
He sits with his nose to the stone all day. North's the other way, but he doesn't know that.
Or he does, and he's being patient.
You knock. From the yard, Mr Pargeter calls that he's out here, and has been since six.
You knock. Nobody answers. There is a light on upstairs.
A tea chest on its side, straw inside, the front knocked out. The straw is pressed down in a round, the size of a tortoise.
Horace, in his box, with his nose to the stone.
A dandelion, bitten down to the stalk. The bite is fresh, and about the width of a tortoise.
Afternoon. Coker. I wall.
Three more stones from the heap would see me to my tea, and my back won't lift them. Flat ones, dressed square. They go in easy.
Three from the heap by the walls, to the gap at the end. Carry them, don't drag them. They mark.
That's the three. Set in nice.
You'll have seen what they are. Face down, they're only stone.
Nobody's using them now. Not since they all got up and went walking.
You carry them back and stand them up by the heap, faces out.
Mr Coker watches you do it and says nothing about it.
It'll be a good wall. It'll go as far as they'll let me have stones.
You stood them up. Suit yourself.
I'll find more. There's plenty lying face down, round here.
A dry-stone wall, knee high, laid well. It goes nowhere in particular, very straight.
A dry-stone wall, knee high, laid well. One stone in it is dressed square, and there are letters cut in the face that meets the next stone: LOVING MEM.
A tin mug of tea, gone cold, with a skin on it. It has been here since morning.
A headstone, stood up by the heap with its face out. The name has worn off in the weather. The dates are still there, and the second one is this year.
Don't knock. Whatever you do.
My Mary's in there. She was out after the bell on Sunday, and she came back wrong. She's to stop in till she's right.
I can't get round the back, not on these feet. Would you look at the boards over the back window? See they're holding.
Round the side, where the back window is. Don't knock.
From the inside. She's been at them all night, then.
She's not to come out. Not till she's right. I've not slept since Sunday, and I'll not start now.
Thank you for looking. Don't knock.
Don't you go talking to her. She'll say anything.
Thank you. Another night, then.
I've new planks. I'll go round again.
He went off before it was light. Barefoot. He didn't look back at the house.
I'll not board the door. Not for anybody. Not for him either, if he comes back.
A pair of men's boots on the step, full to the laces with black water. Nobody has emptied them.
Mr Rook's boots, full to the laces with black water. He has not had them on since you came.
His feet are bare. He walks on them as if they were somebody else's.
Boards over the back window, nailed at every corner. Every nail has been worked half out, from the inside, all of them the same amount.
The door is boarded over, the planks nailed into the frame. From inside, very quietly, somebody is humming.
You knock. Nobody answers. Something inside moves away from the door.
"Is he gone? He goes off after the bell. I don't know where he sleeps."
"Look at his feet, when he's back. He came in on Sunday without his boots, and he's not put them on since. He can't. They don't fit him now."
"Take the boards off. Please. Or don't, and I'll go on waiting."
You pull the boards off, one by one. The nails come easily. They were most of the way out already.
The door opens a hand's width. "Thank you," she says. "I'll wait for morning. I'd rather see him in the light."
You leave the boards where they are.
After a while, something heavy is pushed against the inside of the door.
The boards are off. The door stands open a hand's width.
Nobody answers. Something heavy has been pushed against the inside of the door.
The door is boarded over. A new stack of planks stands by it.
New planks, and a tin of nails, bright ones.
The old planks, stacked by the step. The nails in them are bent, and all bent the same way.
You'll have to speak up. There's a good deal of glass between us.
Denholm. Company diver. I want my spanner, and it's in the chest, and the chest is locked.
The key's under the flat stone by the step, where I always leave it. I can't bend in this. Nobody can.
Under the flat stone. Shove it over, don't lift it. Then the chest.
That's her. Now then.
Not off. On. They've worked loose, sitting here. Tighten them for me, and I'll go back down.
There's somebody at the intake grille, knocking. Three, and a rest, and three. The Company says leave it. I've left it long enough.
You tighten the wing nuts till they will not go. He stands up, heavy, and goes off without looking back.
The pump's hose goes with him along the ground.
The wing nuts come off hard, and then the helmet. There is lake water in the collar.
"That's better," he says. "I can hear it plainer without."
He does not hear you. The faceplate is tight, and fogged on the inside.
Three, and a rest, and three. Hear it? No. You wouldn't. It's not for you.
I'll sit a while. The Company knows where I am.
A diver's air pump in a wooden case: two handles, a wheel, a coil of hose. The hose is dry.
The air pump, with nobody at the handles. Its hose runs off along the ground and out of sight.
Mr Denholm's helmet, on the ground by the step with the faceplate open. There is a little lake water in the bottom of it.
Come up, come up. Mind the scarf. It goes a long way.
I knit a row for everybody who comes up to the door. Always have. My eyes aren't what they were, so I go by the voice.
Read me the newest rows, would you? Off the end, there, over the arm of the chair.
The end over the arm of the chair. The newest are nearest me.
I've not got your name yet. I'll have it by the time you go.
Everybody who comes up to the door. Mr Dunn was the last before you, and that was a while back.
Yours isn't finished. I can finish it, or you can pull it out. It's your row. You say.
Your row's on the arm of the chair. Tell me to finish it, or pull it out yourself. I'll not pull it. I never have pulled one.
There. Finished. You're down, and you're warm.
Take this. Odd ends, but it'll keep the wind off. Your name's in the corner, same as on mine.
You pulled it.
Well. There's a gap now, where you'd be. Nobody has you down anywhere. I hope you know what you're about.
You're down. Come up any time. You'll not get another row, mind. One each.
I've left the gap. I'll not knit over it. Somebody might come back for it.
The newest rows, over the arm of her chair. Plain knitting, with a name worked into each row in a darker wool: SAM ILES. ADA ILES. THE CONSTABLE. MR DUNN.
The last row is only cast on, in the darker wool. There are no letters in it yet.
Your row, cast on, the needles still in it. No letters yet.
Your row, the needles still in it. She says she will finish it with you stood in front of her.
The newest rows. The last one is finished. She went by your voice, she says, and she has it right.
The newest rows. Where your row was there is a gap, and the stitches either side of it do not quite meet.
Mrs Wakes's scarf, lying along the ground in a long run. It goes back to her chair.
The far end of the scarf. The first rows, faded to no colour at all. There are names worked in, too worn to read.
A tangle of pulled wool, still crimped from the needles. Your row.
Nobody comes to the door. Mrs Wakes is out in front, in her chair.
Afternoon. Nothing stops here, but we keep the lamps lit. The Company likes them kept.
They're dry. The oil's in the lamp locker, and a barrel's rolled against it. My back won't shift it. Would yours?
The locker, by the old walls. Push the barrel off the door. It rolls, if you lean on it.
Enough for one lamp. That'll do.
Tonight, after the bell, light the red. Just the red. Red, and the Sunday train runs through without stopping.
The red lamp, after the bell. Not the green. We've no call to stop anything here.
Red. It ran through, then. I heard it.
She's still by the bench. She'll be there next Sunday, and I'll be here, and the lamp will be red.
Green.
I heard it stop in the night. I heard the door go, and I heard it start again.
She's gone, then. I'd have done the same, once.
The lamp's red every night now. I see to it myself.
The bench is empty. I still sweep under it, Sundays.
I'm waiting for the Sunday train.
It hasn't stopped here in eleven years. Not once. I keep the case packed.
He'll want red. Red, and it runs through.
I've a ticket. It's only a single. Green, if you're asked. Green, and it stops, and I get on.
Next Sunday, then.
I'll keep the case packed.
GOLDSKIN MINING Co. LIGHT RAILWAY. BRICKFIELD HALT. SUNDAYS ONLY.
Trains stop here on request. To stop the train, show a green lamp after the bell. A red lamp tells the driver to run through.
A signal lamp on a post, with red glass. It is dry and cold. The lamps here are lit after the bell.
A signal lamp with red glass, dry. You have oil for one lamp.
The red lamp, lit. It burns steady.
The red lamp is dry. The oil went in the green.
A signal lamp on a post, with green glass. It is dry and cold. The lamps here are lit after the bell.
A signal lamp with green glass, dry. You have oil for one lamp.
The green lamp, lit. It burns steady.
The green lamp is dry. The oil went in the red.
Sorrell. Vermin. The Company pays by the head, and there's more heads in these walls than I've eyes for.
Web spinners. Four would do. I'll split it with you, and I'll not say which half.
In the walls, all round. They sit still and spit. Don't stand still and be spat at.
Four. That's four fewer.
Now then. I'll tell you why I leave some.
What's under that hatch lives on them. They drop in, it eats, it stays down. You've had its supper off it.
Here. Scrag end, my own dinner. Down the hatch with it after the bell, before it's up.
Or draw the bolt and be stood there when it comes. I'd not. But you're not me.
The hatch, after the bell. The meat down it, or the bolt back and you stood ready.
Fed, and down. Good. It'll keep a week on that.
Back to spinners, then. I'll leave you a few.
You drew the bolt.
Well. That's the Company's weighbridge with nothing under it, and no call for a vermin man over nothing.
He leans his pole on the wall. "I'll finish the week."
It's quiet down there. Fed things are.
I've leant my pole on the wall. I'll not want it.
A hatch in the floor, bolted from the outside. The bolt is new. The wood round it is scored from underneath.
A hatch in the floor, bolted. Something under it is breathing, slow.
Something pushes up at the hatch from underneath. The bolt holds, just.
Something pushes up at the hatch from underneath. The bolt holds, just.
You draw the bolt a hand's width, push the meat through, and shoot it home again. The pushing stops.
A hatch in the floor, bolted. It is quiet underneath.
The hatch is open. Something came up out of it.
The hatch, open. Underneath, a hole in wet stone goes down further than the light does. Nothing moves in it.
Two cage traps, empty, the doors tied open with string. Nothing he wants to catch alive.
Mr Sorrell's pole, leant on the wall, with nothing tied to it.
